 Two North Dakota residents join federal lawsuit challenging SNAP food restrictions
 by 
 Chris Larson 
 November 21, 2026 
 9:29 am 
 Local News 
 Gavel stock photo: via pexel.com 
 WASHINGTON — Two North Dakota residents are among the plaintiffs in a federal class-action lawsuit challenging restrictions on what Americans can purchase using Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) benefits.
 The lawsuit, filed November 18 in U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, names U.S. Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins and the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) as defendants.
 The 55-page complaint challenges the federal government’s approval of SNAP food restriction waivers in 18 states, including North Dakota. The plaintiffs argue that USDA exceeded its legal authority by allowing states to restrict purchases of certain foods and beverages using SNAP benefits.
 The lawsuit seeks to overturn the restrictions and prevent the federal government from approving similar waivers in the future.
 North Dakota residents among plaintiffs 
 Tamara Wagner of Fargo and James Ness of Bismarck are among the individuals named as plaintiffs in the lawsuit.
 According to the court filing, both rely on SNAP benefits to purchase groceries and say North Dakota’s restrictions have made it more difficult to meet their daily nutritional and personal needs.
 The lawsuit alleges that Wagner has experienced difficulties obtaining products she previously purchased with SNAP benefits. Her attorneys argue that the restrictions have created additional financial challenges and negatively affected her ability to meet essential needs.
 Ness, who resides in a homeless shelter in Bismarck, also says the restrictions have reduced his food purchasing options.
 According to the complaint, Ness has limited access to cooking facilities and depends on ready-to-eat and shelf-stable foods. The lawsuit states that the restrictions have made it more difficult for him to purchase certain products he regularly relies on.
 Both plaintiffs argue that their limited financial resources prevent them from purchasing restricted products using money outside their SNAP benefits.
 North Dakota restrictions took effect November 1 
 According to the court documents, North Dakota initially submitted its request to restrict certain SNAP purchases on October 24, 2025, before submitting a revised proposal on November 3, 2025.
 USDA approved the state’s request on December 10, 2025.
 The restrictions took effect November 1, 2026, prohibiting SNAP benefits from being used to purchase candy, soft drinks and energy drinks.
 The restrictions were approved as part of a federal initiative allowing states to test changes to SNAP purchasing rules.
 However, the plaintiffs argue the restrictions unlawfully change the federal definition of eligible food.
 The lawsuit also alleges that none of the challenged state waivers provides exceptions for individuals who need restricted products because of medical conditions or other personal circumstances.
 Public comments raised concerns 
 North Dakota’s waiver received opposition during the federal public comment process, according to the complaint.
 The filing cites a Federal Register notice acknowledging that most commenters opposed the state’s proposal.
 Concerns included potential negative effects on health and nutrition, reduced consumer choice, additional burdens on SNAP households, confusion among retailers and consumers, and questions about how the program’s effectiveness would be evaluated.
 Despite those objections, USDA allowed North Dakota’s restrictions to proceed without modification.
 The complaint also cites comments from an anonymous North Dakota SNAP recipient who argued that benefits already provide insufficient money to cover many households’ monthly food expenses.
 The commenter warned that restricting eligible purchases could force low-income families to spend more of their limited cash on food, leaving less money for other necessities.
 Lawsuit challenges USDA’s authority 
 The plaintiffs argue that USDA improperly relied on a section of federal law intended to authorize experimental projects that improve SNAP administration and benefit delivery.
 According to the complaint, projects specifically intended to improve recipients’ health and nutrition fall under a different section of federal law with more stringent requirements.
 The lawsuit also claims USDA reversed its previous position on restrictions without adequately explaining why.
 In 2018, the agency rejected similar proposals from Maine and Nevada, citing concerns about increased administrative expenses, burdens on retailers, limitations on consumer choice and a lack of demonstrated health benefits.
 The plaintiffs contend USDA failed to adequately address those concerns when approving the newer waivers.
 The complaint references a separate June 22, 2026, federal court decision in Aragon v. Rollins , which overturned five similar food restriction waivers. The plaintiffs argue the legal reasoning in that decision should also apply to the 18 waivers challenged in the new lawsuit.
 The lawsuit further challenges the federal government’s enforcement framework, which the complaint says allows undercover compliance investigations and could result in retailers losing SNAP authorization for repeated violations.
 Plaintiffs seek nationwide relief 
 The lawsuit requests class-action status on behalf of affected SNAP recipients and asks the court to declare USDA’s approval of the challenged restrictions unlawful.
 The plaintiffs also want the court to block enforcement of restrictions already in effect, prevent approved restrictions from taking effect in other states and prohibit USDA from approving future food restriction waivers under the challenged statutory authority.
 The complaint includes individual SNAP recipients from several states and the South Carolina Convenience & Petroleum Marketers Association, which represents businesses that accept SNAP benefits.
 North Dakota’s SNAP purchasing restrictions remain in effect as the plaintiffs seek a federal court order overturning them.
